title: Can Scientists Grow a New Human Organ?

shots.vo: Right now, more than a hundred thousand people in the United States are waiting for an organ transplant. Someone new is added to the list about every eight minutes. And every day, people die while they're still waiting.

Every day in the United States, around seventeen people on that list die waiting. Around the world, the World Health Organization estimates that only about one in ten people who need a transplant gets one.
But what if we didn't have to wait for a donor? What if doctors could grow you a brand new organ, made from your own cells, one your body would never reject?
It sounds like science fiction. But scientists are already growing simple tissues, printing living structures, and transplanting organs from genetically edited pigs. So how close are we?
The first successful organ transplant happened in 1954, when surgeons in Boston moved a kidney from one identical twin into the other.

The surgeon who led that operation, Joseph Murray, later won the Nobel Prize. Since then, transplants have saved millions of lives. But they've always been limited by two problems: too few donors, and rejection.
The twins mattered, because your immune system is built to attack anything that isn't you. An organ from someone else looks like an invader.

So transplant patients must take drugs that suppress their immune system for the rest of their lives. Those drugs raise the risk of infections and other serious problems, and many donated organs eventually fail anyway.
And even with those drugs, transplanted organs don't last forever. A kidney from a deceased donor often works for somewhere around ten to fifteen years, and then the patient may need another.
An organ grown from your own cells could solve both problems at once. No waiting list, and no rejection.
So why can't we just grow one? Because organs are astonishingly complex. A human heart contains billions of cells, of many different types, arranged in precise layers.

And every one of those cells needs oxygen. In living tissue, cells sit within a fraction of a millimeter of a blood vessel. Grow a thick chunk of tissue without vessels, and the cells in the middle suffocate and die.
That's why the hardest part of growing an organ isn't making the cells. It's building the plumbing: a network of blood vessels that reaches every corner.

Scientists have tried some clever tricks. In 2012, a team printed a lattice of sugar glass inside a gel full of cells, then dissolved the sugar away, leaving open channels that liquid could flow through, like tiny blood vessels.
One of the first big successes came from Doctor Anthony Atala and his team. They built bladder-shaped scaffolds out of material that slowly dissolves in the body.

They coated the scaffolds with cells taken from each patient's own bladder, grew them in the lab, and implanted them. In 2006, they reported that the lab-grown bladders were still working in patients years later.
Bladders are relatively simple, hollow organs. Skin, cartilage and parts of the eye are simpler still, and lab-grown versions of some of these are already being used to treat patients.
Lab-grown skin has been used to help burn victims since the nineteen-eighties. Doctors take a small patch of the patient's skin, grow it into larger sheets, and graft it back on.
For complex organs, scientists found a clever shortcut. In 2008, a team in Minnesota took a rat heart and washed it with detergent until all of its cells were gone.
What was left was a ghostly white framework of proteins, still shaped like a heart, with the outlines of its blood vessels intact.
They filled it with new heart cells, and after about a week, it started to beat. It was weak, but it was a beating heart, rebuilt in a lab.

To build an organ from your own cells, you need the right kinds of cells, and lots of them. In 2006, the Japanese scientist Shinya Yamanaka discovered how to turn ordinary adult cells, like skin cells, back into stem cells, using just four genes.
These induced pluripotent stem cells can become almost any cell type: heart muscle, nerve cells, liver cells, and more. Yamanaka shared the Nobel Prize for this discovery in 2012.
In 2014, doctors in Japan carried out the first transplant of tissue made from these reprogrammed cells: a sheet of retinal cells, grown from a patient's own skin, to treat an eye disease.
Using stem cells, labs now grow organoids: tiny, simplified organs, often smaller than a pea. There are mini-guts, mini-kidneys, mini-livers, and even mini-brains.
They're far too small to transplant. But they're already helping scientists study diseases and test drugs on real human tissue, without risking a patient.
Then there's 3D bioprinting. Instead of plastic, these printers lay down bio-ink: gels packed with living cells, one layer at a time.
In 2019, researchers in Tel Aviv printed a small heart, about the size of a rabbit's, using a patient's own cells and tissue. It even had blood vessels.
It couldn't pump yet. But it showed that one day, we might be able to print organs that match each patient perfectly.
Printing a full-size organ is a much bigger challenge. A human heart or kidney needs billions of cells, and they all have to stay alive while the printer works, which can take hours.
While lab-grown organs are still years away, another approach is moving fast: borrowing organs from pigs.
Pig organs are about the right size for people. But a normal pig organ would be destroyed by the human immune system, very quickly.

So scientists use CRISPR to edit the pigs' genes. They remove sugars that trigger rejection, add human genes, and switch off ancient viruses hidden in pig DNA. One line of pigs carries sixty-nine edits.
Some of these pigs carry dozens of genetic changes. One pig kidney transplanted in 2024 had sixty-nine edits, most of them to switch off old virus genes hidden in the pig's DNA.
In 2022, a man in Maryland named David Bennett became the first person to receive a heart from a gene-edited pig. He lived for about two months.
In 2024, surgeons began transplanting gene-edited pig kidneys into living patients. One woman lived with her pig kidney for more than four months before it had to be removed.
And in 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration cleared the first clinical trials of pig kidney transplants. What was once science fiction is now being tested in real patients.
Some scientists are trying something even stranger: growing human organs inside animals. By adding human stem cells to animal embryos, they hope to one day grow a human kidney inside a pig.
In 2023, researchers in China reported early pig embryos with developing kidney tissue made mostly of human cells. It's very early research, and it raises serious ethical questions.

This raises big ethical questions. How should these animals be treated? And how much human tissue is acceptable inside another species? Scientists and regulators are setting strict limits as the research moves forward.
So, can scientists grow a new human organ? Simple tissues, yes. A full, working heart or kidney grown from scratch? Not yet.
The biggest hurdles are building blood vessels, getting billions of cells to organize themselves the right way, and keeping everything alive long enough to work.

Some researchers are also asking whether we could help the body regrow organs itself. The liver already does this. Remove a large part of it, and the rest can grow back to nearly full size within months.
But the pieces are coming together: stem cells, scaffolds, organoids, printers, and edited pig organs. Within a few decades, the transplant waiting list could start to disappear.

vo: Maybe one day, a new organ will be something you order, not something you wait for.
